children.name: Isis anastatica Linnaeus, 1758
children.description: Hydram refert compositam in formam Anastaticae, sed adeo parva, ut vix nudis adpareat oculis; singulum quemque ramulum terminat Hydra s. flosculus sentiens, & ad minimum motum contrahuntur omnes in globum more Anastaticae siccae; mortuis animalculis restat stirps ramosa, rigida, dum ad tactum tantum sentitur scabrities, quae oculo armato fruticulum refert.

children.name: Isis hippuris Linnaeus, 1758
children.description: Isis hippuris, also known as sea bamboo (though this common name is ambiguous), is a species of bamboo coral found in the Western Pacific Ocean, commonly near the coasts of Indonesia.

children.name: Rumphella aggregata
children.description: Justification: These Indian records seem to be either invalid or unconfirmable: Kumar et al. 2014 a: 56, pl. 25, fig. A – D (Andaman and Nicobar Islands); Fernando et al. 2017: 220, pl. 101, fig. A – D (Andaman and Nicobar Islands. Literature analysis: This species was originally erected by Nuttting as Plexaura aggregata for a specimen from Indonesia, and was later transferred to the new genus Rumphella by Bayer (1955). There are obvious differences between the traits of this species and those of the material described in the accounts (both identical) given by Kumar et al. (2014 a) and Fernando et al. (2017). In the Indian papers the colonies are described as having thick, “ whip-like ” branches with blunt tips, which somewhat matches the illustration of the collected specimen where the terminal branches actually appear to be thin and tapered (“ whip-like ”). This is all in contrast to the non-tapering branches of R. aggregata with their characteristsic clavate tips as shown in Nutting’s figure (1910 a: pl. 1, fig. 1). The colony in the underwater photograph in the Indian papers does not appear to be the same as the collected specimen and looks more like a Hicksonella. The Indian material is also described as being “ dirty white to grey in colour when live ”. The species is photosynthetic and so this is possibly the colour when colonies have their polyps extended.

children.name: Rumphella torta
children.description: Justification: These Indian records seem to be either invalid or unconfirmable: Kumar et al. 2014 a: 58, pl. 26, fig. A – E (Andaman and Nicobar Islands); Fernando et al. 2017: 222, pl. 106, fig. A – E (Andaman and Nicobar Islands). Literature analysis: This species, originally named Plexaura torta, forms large bushy colonies with long drooping end branches. The descriptions of an Indian specimen given by Kumar et al. (2014 a) and Fernando et al. (2017) are identical but it is difficult to tell whether their material is the same as this taxon because, although their colony looks like this species, the authors only figure nine sclerites (two of which are identical) and most of sclerite forms that are well illustrated by Grasshoff (2000) are not included in their figure. This species has only been reported from the Red Sea and East Africa. Kumar et al. (2015, 2018) lists the species and presents one of the colony images from the 2014 and 2017 papers above. Kumar et al. (2019 b) lists the species with a colony image, while Kumar et al. (2018 a) just lists the species.

children.name: Hicksonella princeps Nutting, 1910
children.description: Justification: These Indian records seem to be either invalid or unconfirmable: Kumar et al. 2014 a: 60, pl. 27, fig. A – E (Guitor Island); Fernando et al. 2017: 218, pl. 100, fig. A – E (Guitor Island). Literature analysis: The descriptions given by Kumar et al. (2014 a) and Fernando et al. (2017) are identical but the sclerites that are illustrated are quite different from those of H. princeps as figured by Alderslade (1986: fig. 6). In the latter figure, the warts on the clubs and the short, slender spindles are spiny, and on the spindles, there are three of these warts in each of two conspicuous, opposed, median girdles. Sclerites like these are also characteristic of Rumphella aggregata (Nutting, 1910) (see Bayer 1955: fig. 2 a). None of the spindles figured in the Indian papers are of this form, and the second sclerite from the left of the “ subsurface ” sclerites, an oval spindle with numerous girdles of rounded warts, has not been reported for any species of Hicksonella. Kumar et al. (2015) just listed the species and provided an image of the specimen from the 2014 and 2017 papers above. This species has only been reported from Indonesia, New Caledonia and Australia.
